t: Count Common Words With One Occurrence: Frequency Maps Done Right
o:
**Understanding the problem**

Count strings that occur exactly once in `words1` AND exactly once in `words2`. In Example 1, "leetcode" and "amazing" qualify; "is" fails (twice in `words1`) and "as" fails (absent from `words2`), so the answer is 2. Example 3 shows the asymmetry trap: "a" appears in both arrays but three times in `words2`, leaving only "ab". Constraints are tiny (1000 words of up to 30 letters), so even repeated full scans fit easily; the interesting part is choosing a clean formulation.
k: Two conditions must hold simultaneously: frequency exactly 1 in words1 and exactly 1 in words2.
Building a Counter per array reduces the answer to one intersection scan over map entries.
Words are compared exactly (case-sensitive lowercase), so hashing on the raw string is correct.

a.i: For each distinct candidate word from words1, count its occurrences in both arrays with full scans and keep it only when both counts equal 1. A seen-set prevents counting a duplicated word of words1 twice.
s: Iterate words1, skipping words already processed (seen set).
Count occurrences of the word in words1 and in words2.
Increment the answer iff both counts are exactly 1.
a.t: O(n * (n + m) * L) - each candidate rescans both arrays; L bounds per-comparison string cost

a.i: Hash-count both arrays in one pass each. The answer is the number of words whose count is 1 in both maps; scanning either map enumerates all candidates exactly once.
s: Build map c1 from words1 and c2 from words2.
Count entries with frequency 1 in c1 and frequency exactly 1 in c2 (absent means 0).
a.t: O((n + m) * L) - one counting pass per array plus one map scan
a.sp: O((n + m) * L) - both frequency maps

w:
**Wrap-up**

Use the two-map solution; the brute force is only worth mentioning to note the constraints forgive it. Pitfalls: requiring presence rather than exact-once presence (Example 3), and double-counting duplicate words when brute forcing. Generalization: k arrays reduce to requiring frequency 1 in all k maps - still linear. Related warm-ups include counting common words regardless of multiplicity.
